description: Curriculum topic bank for reading content generation, aligned with WIDA ELP levels 1–6. Topics increase in cognitive and linguistic complexity as students progress. Each level maps to a proficiency band and provides topic categories, specific topics, text types, and vocabulary tiers appropriate for that level.

levels.complexityNote: Grade 6–8 content in illustrated text (1–3 labeled pictures with captions) or simple charts and environmental print. Single nouns and action verbs, highly repetitive patterns. Students identify or match information from short visual-supported text.

topics: parts of a plant: roots, stem, leaves, flower, seed
animal body parts: eyes, ears, fins, wings, claws
food groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, proteins, dairy
types of animals: mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, insects
human body: bones, muscles, heart, lungs, brain
types of weather: sunny, rainy, cloudy, snowy, windy
landforms: mountain, valley, river, ocean, desert
seasons: spring, summer, fall, winter
sky objects: sun, moon, stars, clouds
natural resources: water, air, soil, rocks, plants
school community roles: teacher, principal, librarian, nurse, coach
types of maps: world map, country map, city map, classroom map
transportation: car, bus, train, airplane, boat
community helpers: police, firefighter, doctor, farmer, mail carrier
national symbols: flag, eagle, Statue of Liberty, White House
geometric shapes: circle, square, triangle, rectangle, hexagon
measurement tools: ruler, scale, thermometer, measuring cup, clock
money: penny, nickel, dime, quarter, dollar
simple graphs: bar graph, picture graph, tally chart
number line: counting, ordering, comparing numbers

levels.complexityNote: Grade 6–8 content in simple 2–4 sentence texts with illustrations or graphic organizers. Familiar academic phrases, simple present and past tense, Tier-1 and basic Tier-2 vocabulary. Students locate main ideas and sequence events from short passages.

topics: the water cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection
weather patterns: temperature, precipitation, wind speed
natural disasters: earthquakes, volcanoes, and floods — what causes them
renewable vs. non-renewable energy: solar, wind, coal, oil
environmental vs. genetic factors in plant traits
food chains: producers, consumers, and decomposers
plant adaptations to different environments: desert, rainforest, arctic
animal life cycles: egg, larva, pupa, adult
the digestive system: how food moves through the body
inherited vs. learned traits in animals
timeline of a U.S. historical event: sequence of causes and effects
immigration: reasons people move and the steps involved
how a bill becomes a law: the basic sequence of steps
comparing two world regions: climate, population, main resources
roles of local, state, and federal government
story settings: identifying time, place, and context from a passage
cause and effect in a short story
character problem and solution in a narrative
comparing two characters based on their actions
point of view: first-person vs. third-person narration

levels.complexityNote: Grade 6–8 leveled text in short paragraphs (4–6 sentences). Subject-area vocabulary with context clues. Students identify main ideas and details, make simple inferences, and recognize basic text structure.

topics: states of matter: solid, liquid, gas, and how they change
force and motion: how push and pull affect objects
simple machines: lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle
light and shadow: reflection, refraction, and transparent vs. opaque
magnetism: poles, attraction, repulsion, and everyday uses
ecosystems: how living and non-living things interact
photosynthesis: how plants make food from sunlight
rock cycle: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic — how rocks form and change
ocean zones: intertidal, neritic, open ocean, deep sea
human impact on the environment: pollution, deforestation, conservation
the American Revolution: causes, key events, outcomes
three branches of U.S. government: powers and checks and balances
geography of the Americas: mountains, rivers, climate zones
ancient civilizations: Egypt, Greece, or Rome — achievements and daily life
the Civil War: causes, major battles, and Reconstruction
identifying theme in a short story using text evidence
comparing narrative and informational text on the same topic
author's purpose: to inform, persuade, or entertain
figurative language: simile, metaphor, and personification in context
text features: headings, captions, bold words, diagrams

levels.complexityNote: Grade 6–8 multi-paragraph text (2–3 paragraphs) with moderate Tier-2 academic vocabulary. Students identify relationships between main ideas and details, draw inferences, and analyze text structure.

topics: the immune system: how the body defends against pathogens
plate tectonics: continental drift, earthquakes, and volcanic activity
genetic inheritance: dominant and recessive traits
chemical vs. physical changes: properties and examples
the nitrogen cycle: how nitrogen moves through ecosystems
westward expansion: Manifest Destiny, the Oregon Trail, conflicts with Native Americans
the Industrial Revolution: inventions, urbanization, and working conditions
World War I: causes, major powers, and consequences
the civil rights movement: key figures, events, and legislation
economic systems: capitalism, socialism — comparing structures
analyzing a character's motivation using text evidence
comparing theme across two short literary passages
evaluating an author's argument: claims, evidence, and reasoning
comparing primary and secondary sources on the same event
irony and symbolism in grade-level fiction
mental health awareness: recognizing stress and coping strategies
media literacy: identifying bias and evaluating sources
nutrition science: macronutrients, micronutrients, and healthy choices
cyberbullying: causes, effects, and prevention strategies
climate change: evidence, causes, and proposed solutions

levels.complexityNote: Grade 6–8 extended text (3–5 paragraphs) from multiple perspectives or sources. Higher-register academic vocabulary, complex sentence structures. Students sequence main ideas, evaluate evidence, and compare across texts.

topics: CRISPR gene editing: how it works, benefits, and ethical debates
artificial intelligence: current applications and societal implications
renewable energy transition: solar, wind, and grid challenges
space exploration: Mars missions — rationale, risks, and costs
antibiotic resistance: causes, global impact, and solutions
comparing causes and effects of World War I and World War II
the Cold War: ideological conflict, proxy wars, and the arms race
globalization: economic benefits and cultural consequences
democracy vs. authoritarianism: comparing governance systems
the Harlem Renaissance: art, literature, and the Great Migration
comparing an author's perspective across two essays on the same issue
evaluating the reliability of digital news sources
dystopian fiction: how authors use setting to critique society
structural choices in expository writing: argument vs. explanation
rhetorical appeals: ethos, pathos, logos in persuasive texts
supply and demand: how markets determine prices
immigration policy: debates around enforcement and reform
the role of the Supreme Court in shaping civil rights
economic inequality: causes, data, and policy responses
entrepreneurship and innovation: case studies of young entrepreneurs

levels.complexityNote: Complex grade-level text (4+ paragraphs) with nuanced academic vocabulary, diverse text types including charts, tables, and multimedia sources. Students evaluate central ideas, identify bias, distinguish fact from speculation, and synthesize across sources.

topics: climate modeling: how scientists predict future warming and its limitations
neuroscience of learning: how memory consolidation works
evolution and natural selection: evidence across time scales
biotechnology and ethics: GMOs, cloning, and genetic privacy
quantum computing: principles and potential real-world disruptions
colonialism's long-term economic effects on developing nations
the United Nations: structure, successes, and limitations
comparative constitutional systems: U.S., UK, and parliamentary democracies
genocide and international justice: Nuremberg to the ICC
identity and nationalism: how nations define citizenship and belonging
Shakespeare's use of language to reflect Elizabethan society
postcolonial literature: themes of identity and resistance
how narrative perspective shapes reader sympathy in a novel
evaluating conflicting critical interpretations of a poem
the evolution of argument structure in American political speeches
